Includes chart on retail and counterfactual fuel prices showing subsidy impact. Critical data: headline inflation 7.4% end-2021, 8.7% by August 2022; food inflation 14.1% August 2022 (accounting for over 50% of excess inflation above target); core inflation 8.1%. Fuel subsidies increased to contain energy price inflation. Near-term inflation expectations above upper target limit, medium-term rising, longer-term stable.","exclusion_reason":null},{"schema_version":"chunk_routing_decision_v1","source_id":"MAC-010","source_sha256":"8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a","chunk_id":"unit-0010","included":true,"relevant_question_ids":["5B.2","5B.3","5B.7","5B.9"],"relevance_strength":"material","adjacent_chunk_ids":["unit-0009","unit-0011","unit-0012","unit-0016","unit-0017"],"explanation":"This chunk covers monetary policy response (paragraphs 6-7) and financial conditions. Banco de México (Banxico) responded to inflationary pressures with accelerating pace of tightening: 25bp initial hikes, then 50bp, then 75bp when inflation became broad-based. Policy rate at 9.25%, about 6 percentage points above U.S. Fed rate. Financial Conditions Index showing moderate tightening to levels below past peaks. Interest rates on peso-denominated debt at highest since Global Financial Crisis; 1-year government bond yield risen 250bps vs 100bps for 20-year bond; real yield on inflation-linked Udibonos rising. This documents the monetary governance response to inflation shock (5B.9) and institutional independence (5B.2).","exclusion_reason":null},{"schema_version":"chunk_routing_decision_v1","source_id":"MAC-010","source_sha256":"8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a","chunk_id":"unit-0011","included":true,"relevant_question_ids":["5B.3","5B.4","5B.5","5B.7","5B.9"],"relevance_strength":"material","adjacent_chunk_ids":["unit-0010","unit-0012","unit-0013","unit-0022","unit-0025"],"explanation":"This chunk continues financial conditions discussion (paragraphs 7-8) including foreign-currency denominated securities yields, sovereign risk spreads, and peso stability. Gross international reserves slightly declined from SDR allocation peak but remain adequate (ARA metric coverage 125%). Charts show exchange rates vs U.S. dollar, market implied inflation breakevens, and portfolio flows. This documents financial market integrity and external sector governance.","exclusion_reason":null},{"schema_version":"chunk_routing_decision_v1","source_id":"MAC-010","source_sha256":"8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a","chunk_id":"unit-0012","included":true,"relevant_question_ids":["5B.2","5B.3","5B.6","5B.8","5B.9"],"relevance_strength":"material","adjacent_chunk_ids":["unit-0011","unit-0013","unit-0014","unit-0025","unit-0049","unit-0055"],"explanation":"This chunk covers credit growth recovery, banking system health, and PEMEX performance (paragraphs 9-13). Bank credit recovering despite tighter conditions; loans to households picked up earlier led by public non-bank mortgage lending. Banking system: capital adequacy ratio increased to over 19% from 16% pre-pandemic; large institutions maintain ample liquidity buffers. PEMEX earnings doubled to over USD 23 billion in H1 2022 (EBITDA basis) due to higher oil prices and modest production increase, allowing rise in capital expenditures but mostly for debt amortization; total debt remains high. This documents financial sector institutional quality and state enterprise governance (5B.2, 5B.6).","exclusion_reason":null},{"schema_version":"chunk_routing_decision_v1","source_id":"MAC-010","source_sha256":"8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a","chunk_id":"unit-0013","included":true,"relevant_question_ids":["5B.1","5B.3","5B.6","5B.8","5B.9","5B.10"],"relevance_strength":"pivotal","adjacent_chunk_ids":["unit-0012","unit-0014","unit-0015","unit-0019","unit-0020","unit-0025","unit-0043","unit-0046","unit-0048","unit-0049","unit-0050"],"explanation":"This chunk covers OUTLOOK AND RISKS (paragraphs 13-17) and Box 1 on the 2023 Budget Proposal. Staff projects growth of 2.1% in 2022 and 1.2% in 2023 with weakening domestic and U.S. demand. Inflation projected to plateau at ~8.5% in H2 2022 then gradually decline, returning to midpoint of 3% target band in mid-2024 assuming policy rate ~10% by early 2023. Balance of risks tilted to downside: higher global inflation, sharper tightening of global financial conditions, sharper deceleration in U.S. growth, supply shocks, pandemic variants, climate risks. Upside: nearshoring continuation, smaller U.S. spillovers. Box 1 shows 2023 budget: revenue 24.1% GDP, expenditure 28.2% GDP, overall balance -4.1% GDP, interest payments 4.6% GDP, fuel subsidy 0% (after 0.5% in 2022), primary balance 0.3% GDP.","exclusion_reason":null},{"schema_version":"chunk_routing_decision_v1","source_id":"MAC-010","source_sha256":"8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a","chunk_id":"unit-0014","included":true,"relevant_question_ids":["5B.1","5B.3","5B.6","5B.7","5B.8","5B.9","5B.10"],"relevance_strength":"material","adjacent_chunk_ids":["unit-0013","unit-0015","unit-0016","unit-0019","unit-0020","unit-0025","unit-0085"],"explanation":"This chunk continues OUTLOOK discussion (paragraphs 15-17) including growth trajectory assessment (potential output per capita recovering to slightly above 1% without structural reforms), current account deficit stabilizing at ~1% GDP medium term, and detailed risk enumeration. Risks categorized: external (global inflation, financial tightening, U.S. growth), domestic (inflation persistence, backward-looking price dynamics, new COVID variants, climate), medium-term (pandemic scarring, policy uncertainty lowering potential output, climate-induced risks). Authorities' views: budget contemplates 2023 growth 1.2-3.0% (central 2.1%), Banxico forecast 0.8-2.4% (central 1.6%). Inflation falling 2023 under normalization of supply shocks, fiscal measures, decisive monetary policy. U.S. slowdown headline risk but manufacturing sector might be less affected than services.","exclusion_reason":null},{"schema_version":"chunk_routing_decision_v1","source_id":"MAC-010","source_sha256":"8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a","chunk_id":"unit-0015","included":true,"relevant_question_ids":["5B.9","5B.10"],"relevance_strength":"material","adjacent_chunk_ids":["unit-0014","unit-0016","unit-0017","unit-0022"],"explanation":"This chunk completes the OUTLOOK AND RISKS section with authorities' views (paragraph 18). The authorities agreed elevated uncertainty with risks tilted to downside given high global and domestic interest rates, high inflation, and downside growth risks. They noted manufacturing sector bulk of trade exposure might be less affected by U.S. slowdown than services, expected nearshoring benefits, and that faster-than-expected global monetary tightening could spark capital flow pressures but experience through tightening cycle so far attenuates concerns. This documents official government perspective on shock vulnerability and management approach.","exclusion_reason":null},{"schema_version":"chunk_routing_decision_v1","source_id":"MAC-010","source_sha256":"8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a","chunk_id":"unit-0016","included":true,"relevant_question_ids":["5B.9","5B.10"],"relevance_strength":"material","adjacent_chunk_ids":["unit-0015","unit-0017","unit-0018","unit-0019","unit-0080"],"explanation":"This chunk is Box 2: Global Tightening and Inflation Scenario simulating downside shocks to Mexican economy using IMF's G20MOD multi-country DSGE model. Three-layer simulation: (1) oil and food price shock (10% and 50% above baseline) raising headline inflation ~1% above elevated baseline; (2) commodity shock causing dislocation of inflation expectations globally, sharper domestic policy rate increase, output falling >1% below baseline peaking in H1 2023; (3) additional 1% domestic demand decline bringing output >2% below baseline at trough while attenuating price pressures. Three layers present substantial cumulative pressure on corporate interest rates. This provides model-based evidence of shock vulnerability and the consequentiality of policy response failures (5B.9).","exclusion_reason":null},{"schema_version":"chunk_routing_decision_v1","source_id":"MAC-010","source_sha256":"8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a","chunk_id":"unit-0017","included":true,"relevant_question_ids":["5B.2","5B.3","5B.7","5B.9"],"relevance_strength":"pivotal","adjacent_chunk_ids":["unit-0016","unit-0018","unit-0019","unit-0020","unit-0021","unit-0025","unit-0080"],"explanation":"This chunk is the start of POLICY DISCUSSIONS Section A: Tackling High Inflation - Monetary Policy (paragraphs 19-22). Banxico proactive approach: since June 2021 successive gradually larger rate increases (25bp initial, then 50bp, then 75bp) brought ex ante real policy rate to moderately restrictive ~4% by September 2022. Charts show inflation and expectations and real ex-ante policy rates. Staff assessment: proactive and appropriately calibrated response to upward inflation surprises and sequential delays in returning to target. Policy rate of at least 10% required for inflation to reverse to 3% target within two years. Inflation risks expected to remain heightened with significant uncertainty about timing, speed, and durability of downward path. Risks: further food/commodity shocks, imported inflation persistence, supply chain pressures, minimum wage increases feeding into costs, more frequent domestic price adjustments, further upticks in near-term expectations.","exclusion_reason":null},{"schema_version":"chunk_routing_decision_v1","source_id":"MAC-010","source_sha256":"8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a","chunk_id":"unit-0018","included":true,"relevant_question_ids":["5B.2","5B.3","5B.7","5B.8","5B.9"],"relevance_strength":"material","adjacent_chunk_ids":["unit-0017","unit-0019","unit-0020","unit-0021","unit-0025","unit-0031"],"explanation":"This chunk continues Monetary Policy discussion (paragraphs 20-22) including risk assessment calling for further rate increases and maintenance at higher level. Asymmetric upside risks to inflation in one-to-two-year monetary policy horizon given backward-looking elements in Mexico's inflation process (Philips curve estimates). Risk management approach requires real ex ante policy rate peaking at over 5% in 2023, broadly consistent with market expectations and staff inflation forecast. Clear monetary policy communication recommended to increase effectiveness: publication of updated inflation forecasts with every rate decision since August 2021, guidance on direction of next policy rate change in monetary policy statement. Recommendation: publish more information on policy rate path underlying macro forecast including expected rate and length of stay at peak and possible policy change triggers. Broader review of Banxico's inflation targeting framework two decades suggested for further improvements.","exclusion_reason":null},{"schema_version":"chunk_routing_decision_v1","source_id":"MAC-010","source_sha256":"8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a","chunk_id":"unit-0019","included":true,"relevant_question_ids":["5B.1","5B.3","5B.6","5B.8","5B.9"],"relevance_strength":"pivotal","adjacent_chunk_ids":["unit-0018","unit-0020","unit-0021","unit-0023","unit-0024","unit-0031","unit-0085","unit-0086"],"explanation":"This chunk covers Fiscal Measures (paragraphs 23-25). Authorities used largely untargeted subsidies to mitigate cost of living rises totaling ~2% GDP including: (1) Retail fuel price stabilization directly reducing cost pressures, lowering inflation estimated 2 percentage points in 2022, at budgetary cost ~1.5% GDP, disproportionately benefiting higher income households and diluting price signals; (2) Food price mitigation at smaller budgetary cost leveraging preexisting programs (fertilizer to small farmers, support for subsistence farming, increased emphasis). Overall fiscal and redistributive measures helped support real incomes; deficit increased only ~0.25% GDP with fuel subsidies offset by higher oil revenues. Administration increased universal social pensions and projected minimum wage from 42% of median formal sector wage in 2018 to 59% in 2022. Real per capita labor income increased ~5% y/y by mid-2022. This directly addresses 5B.8 (distribution fairness) and 5B.9 (shock response quality).","exclusion_reason":null},{"schema_version":"chunk_routing_decision_v1","source_id":"MAC-010","source_sha256":"8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a","chunk_id":"unit-0020","included":true,"relevant_question_ids":["5B.1","5B.3","5B.6","5B.8","5B.9"],"relevance_strength":"material","adjacent_chunk_ids":["unit-0019","unit-0021","unit-0022","unit-0023","unit-0024","unit-0025","unit-0085"],"explanation":"This chunk continues authorities' views on fiscal measures (paragraphs 26-27). Authorities emphasized fuel price stabilization central to supporting households and restraining inflation in line with President's commitment; highlighted analysis suggesting pricing mechanism has dampening second-round inflation effects. Other anti-inflation measures leveraged existing policies in agriculture and basic necessities. Authorities underscored main goal was to support historically underserved agricultural communities with positive effects on agricultural yields. However, note tension: continuing large minimum wage increases will likely add to inflation pressures working counter-purpose to monetary and fiscal policies and potentially reducing formal employment for lower income workers. This documents governance trade-offs and implementation quality issues.","exclusion_reason":null},{"schema_version":"chunk_routing_decision_v1","source_id":"MAC-010","source_sha256":"8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a","chunk_id":"unit-0021","included":true,"relevant_question_ids":["5B.1","5B.3","5B.6","5B.7","5B.8","5B.9","5B.10"],"relevance_strength":"material","adjacent_chunk_ids":["unit-0020","unit-0022","unit-0023","unit-0024","unit-0025","unit-0028","unit-0029","unit-0046","unit-0083","unit-0084","unit-0085"],"explanation":"This chunk covers Section B: Managing Potential Downside Risks - Fiscal Policy (paragraphs 28-30). Fiscal policy could better prepare for downside risks; neutral stance appropriate for modest slowdown but more could be done to prepare targeted support for poorer households. Under Mexico's fiscal framework (balanced budget rule + constraints on debt issuance), scope for countercyclical fiscal policy is limited. Recommendations: (1) Change retail fuel price regime to create room for targeted support when oil prices rise by allowing passthrough, encouraging greener energy transition, reducing budgetary cost of subsidies; (2) Implement proposed reforms to fiscal framework to rebuild FEIP stabilization fund to ~0.3-0.5% GDP. Medium-term: reform needs explicit debt anchor with narrowly defined escape clauses and clear mechanism to return to debt path. This addresses institutional quality of fiscal governance (5B.3) and shock preparedness (5B.9).","exclusion_reason":null},{"schema_version":"chunk_routing_decision_v1","source_id":"MAC-010","source_sha256":"8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a","chunk_id":"unit-0022","included":true,"relevant_question_ids":["5B.3","5B.8","5B.9"],"relevance_strength":"material","adjacent_chunk_ids":["unit-0021","unit-0023","unit-0024","unit-0025","unit-0033","unit-0057"],"explanation":"This chunk continues fiscal policy discussion with authorities' views (paragraphs 31-32) and External Sector Policies (paragraph 32-33). Authorities prefer maintaining current retail fuel price stabilization given President's pledge that fuel prices will not rise in real terms above November 2018 level and legal basis of pricing mechanism. Authorities interested in fiscal framework reforms enabling allocation of fiscal savings and funding from debt issuance to stabilization fund. External sector: peso faced less downward pressure than other EM currencies due to high interest rate differential, strong remittances, fiscal discipline track record, nearshoring inflows. Floating exchange rate should act as shock absorber; FX markets deep and liquid with no significant FX mismatches in balance sheets. If large shock triggers market illiquidity, temporary FX intervention could be considered. FCL provides additional external buffer. This documents institutional approach to macroeconomic stability.","exclusion_reason":null},{"schema_version":"chunk_routing_decision_v1","source_id":"MAC-010","source_sha256":"8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a","chunk_id":"unit-0023","included":true,"relevant_question_ids":["5B.3","5B.5","5B.7"],"relevance_strength":"material","adjacent_chunk_ids":["unit-0022","unit-0024","unit-0025","unit-0026","unit-0027","unit-0042","unit-0088"],"explanation":"This chunk covers Section C: Maintaining a Robust Financial System (paragraphs 35-37) and starts Financial Sector Policies. Financial system emerged from pandemic in good health: NPLs rose modestly from low levels then began declining; capital adequacy ratios high and rising; liquidity ratios comfortable. Systemic vulnerabilities and liquidity risks broadly contained given high capital buffers, low private sector leverage, no sign of stretched asset prices. Bank loans and NFC financial health should be monitored in context of rapid rate rise. NFC average loan rate and 6-month average of 5-yr TIIE swap chart. Mexico's bank regulator CNBV should continue improving supervisory techniques, simplify risk-based rating system, enable effective consolidated supervision of financial conglomerates. This documents institutional quality of financial regulation.","exclusion_reason":null},{"schema_version":"chunk_routing_decision_v1","source_id":"MAC-010","source_sha256":"8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a","chunk_id":"unit-0024","included":true,"relevant_question_ids":["5B.2","5B.3","5B.5","5B.7"],"relevance_strength":"pivotal","adjacent_chunk_ids":["unit-0023","unit-0025","unit-0026","unit-0027","unit-0042","unit-0088"],"explanation":"This chunk continues Financial System discussion (paragraphs 37-41) with detailed recommendations for policy steps to enhance resilience. Key recommendations: (1) Capacity of regulatory agencies: autonomy and resources of regulatory government agencies and legal protection of supervisors could be strengthened; (2) Banking supervision: continue improving techniques (principles- vs rules-based), enable consolidated supervision of all financial conglomerates (currently voluntary); (3) Systemic liquidity management: conditions bear continued monitoring especially with high levels of short-term wholesale funding of development banks; Banxico Emergency Liquidity Assistance framework could be enhanced; (4) Safety nets: closely monitor loan concentration risks and contingent credit lines; strengthen bank resolution and recovery; fill IPAB board vacancies; (5) Cybersecurity: Banxico and CNBV enhance approach to strengthening cybersecurity; (6) Climate risks: exposure manageable but financial tail risks will worsen without resilience investments. Also: AML/CFT regime strengthening, beneficial ownership register, fintech monitoring, CBDC development for financial inclusion.","exclusion_reason":null},{"schema_version":"chunk_routing_decision_v1","source_id":"MAC-010","source_sha256":"8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a","chunk_id":"unit-0025","included":true,"relevant_question_ids":["5B.3","5B.7","5B.9"],"relevance_strength":"material","adjacent_chunk_ids":["unit-0024","unit-0026","unit-0027","unit-0028","unit-0029","unit-0030","unit-0042","unit-0057"],"explanation":"This chunk continues authorities' views on financial system (paragraph 42) and starts Section D: Policies for Higher and More Equitable Growth (paragraphs 43-44). Authorities: committed to monitoring and containing emerging systemic risks; shared view financial system robust and resilient; consider policy framework performed well during pandemic; intend to continue strengthening risk-based supervisory framework and take note of consolidated supervision recommendations. Did not fully share concern on contingent credit lines risks (vast majority revocable) or liquidity risks from development banks (fully backed by sovereign).
